label: Catastrophic risk: chances, sizes and the future a catastrophe could cost

rows.label: World population in the long run (people alive in a typical future year)

source.title: United Nations, Global Issues: Population (World Population Prospects 2024)
source.quote: After reaching this peak, it is expected to gradually decline to around 10.2 billion by the century's end.

rows.explainer: People alive in each future year, the yearly stream of healthy life a catastrophe that shrinks or ends humanity's future would cost: the UN's 2100 projection as the best guess (after its peak of about 10.3 billion in the mid-2080s). The range is ours: a lower population if decline continues past 2100, a higher one if it doesn't. Every model's future loss is this stream of people not yet born, discounted at the shared rate (your discount rate is how much future generations count): the people alive now are counted as deaths, so the stream counts only those born later, rising over a lifetime (life_expectancy_now) to this level.

rows.label: Yearly chance of a pandemic as deadly as COVID-19

source.title: Duke Global Health Institute, Statistics say large pandemics are more likely than we thought (Marani, Katul, Pan and Parolari 2021, PNAS)
source.quote: It found the probability of a pandemic with similar impact to COVID-19 is about 2% in any year

rows.explainer: From four centuries of epidemic records, the yearly chance of a novel pandemic with COVID-19's intensity. The range is ours: half to twice the estimate, since the authors find new outbreaks becoming more frequent and the record is patchy. Read together with covid_excess_deaths, the size of the pandemic it describes.

rows.label: Deaths in a COVID-scale pandemic (WHO excess deaths, 2020-2021)

source.title: World Health Organization, 14.9 million excess deaths associated with the COVID-19 pandemic in 2020 and 2021 (5 May 2022)
source.quote: between 1 January 2020 and 31 December 2021 was approximately 14.9 million (range 13.3 million to 16.6 million)

rows.explainer: Deaths directly or indirectly caused by COVID-19 in its first two years: the size of the pandemic whose yearly chance is pandemic_probability_covid_scale. WHO's range.

rows.label: Share of new infectious diseases whose emergence land-use change drove (since 1960)

source.title: Future Earth, New IPBES report on escaping the pandemic era (IPBES Workshop Report on Biodiversity and Pandemics, 2020)
source.quote: The expansion of anthropogenic activities such as deforestation has caused the emergence of more than 30% of new diseases.

rows.explainer: IPBES's expert workshop: land-use change (deforestation, settlement in wild areas, expansion of crops and livestock) drove the emergence of more than 30% of new diseases reported since 1960. The range is ours: an expert synthesis, not a measured share.

rows.label: Year the tournament's forecasts were made

source.title: Forecasting Research Institute, Forecasting Existential Risks: Evidence from a Long-Run Forecasting Tournament (Karger et al., 2023), Tables 2 and 3
source.page: p. 4: the tournament ran from June to October 2022

rows.explainer: The Existential Risk Persuasion Tournament asked in 2022 for the chance of each catastrophe by 2100; a chance by 2100 over the years from 2022 is the yearly chance the catastrophic-risk models use (spread evenly over the years, a simplification: most forecasters put more of the AI risk later).

rows.label: Year the tournament's forecasts run to

source.title: Forecasting Research Institute, Forecasting Existential Risks: Evidence from a Long-Run Forecasting Tournament (Karger et al., 2023), Tables 2 and 3
source.quote: Median forecasts from the XPT on questions of whether AI, pathogens, nuclear war, or non-anthropogenic risks will, by 2100, cause humanity to go extinct.

rows.explainer: The forecasts' horizon; with xpt_forecast_year it turns a chance by 2100 into a yearly chance.

rows.label: AI: chance of a catastrophe (over 10% of people die) per chance of extinction

source.title: Forecasting Research Institute, Forecasting Existential Risks: Evidence from a Long-Run Forecasting Tournament (Karger et al., 2023), Tables 2 and 3

rows.explainer: How many AI catastrophes that kill over a tenth of humanity (extinction included) the tournament expects per AI-caused extinction: the domain experts' 12% over 3% (4), the best guess because the slider "Chance AI ends humanity's future by 2100" starts at their 3%; the superforecasters' 2.13% over 0.38% (5.6) the high end. The slider sets the extinction-level chance; this ratio adds the catastrophes the world survives.

rows.label: Pandemics (engineered and natural): chance one kills over 10% of people by 2100

source.title: Forecasting Research Institute, Forecasting Existential Risks: Evidence from a Long-Run Forecasting Tournament (Karger et al., 2023), Tables 2 and 3

rows.explainer: Engineered plus natural pathogens causing a catastrophe (over 10% of the people alive die within five years; extinction included) by 2100: the domain experts' 3% + 0.85% as the best guess, the superforecasters' 0.8% + 1% the low end, the tops of the experts' intervals (5% + 2%) the high end. The pathogen questions were asked in a one-shot survey after the tournament (footnote 31), not in the tournament itself. The experts' figure as the best guess is the rule the owner set for AI (2026-11-04: the slider starts at the experts' 3%), applied to every area; the superforecasters' lower figure is the range's low end.

rows.label: Nuclear war: chance it kills over 10% of people by 2100

source.title: Forecasting Research Institute, Forecasting Existential Risks: Evidence from a Long-Run Forecasting Tournament (Karger et al., 2023), Tables 2 and 3

rows.explainer: Domain experts' median (8%) as the best guess; superforecasters' 4% the low end; the top of the experts' interval (11%) the high end. Most of the deaths in such a war would come from famine after the smoke cools the climate (nuclear winter), not the blasts. The experts' figure as the best guess is the rule the owner set for AI (2026-11-04: the slider starts at the experts' 3%), applied to every area; the superforecasters' lower figure is the range's low end.

rows.label: Nuclear war: share of people who die in a catastrophe the world survives

source.title: Xia et al. 2022, Global food insecurity and famine from reduced crop, marine fishery and livestock production due to climate disruption from nuclear war soot (Nature Food)
source.note: Xia et al., Table 1: the India-Pakistan wars above the 10% threshold kill 15%, 23%, 33% and 40% of people by famine, the large US-Russia war 81-85%; Rethink Priorities' cross-cause model puts a nuclear catastrophe's intensity at 36-96% of people.

rows.explainer: A nuclear war that kills over 10% of people would do so mostly through famine after the soot cools the climate: our judgment 45%, between Xia et al.'s regional wars above the threshold (15-40%) and a large US-Russia war (81-85%), the range spanning both.

rows.label: Nuclear war: share of a catastrophe's deaths that come from famine

source.title: IPPNW, Nuclear Famine (August 2022), Table 1: adapted from Xia et al. 2022, Nature Food
source.page: p. 4 (PDF page 5), Table 1: direct fatalities and deaths due to famine by the end of year 2
source.quote: 250 weapons detonated 100 kt each 37 Tg 127 million 2.1 billion

rows.explainer: Deaths from famine over all deaths in Xia et al.'s five India-Pakistan wars (direct deaths and famine deaths by the end of year two): 260 million of 287 million (91%), 930 of 982 (95%), 1.4 billion of 1.5 (94%), 2.1 of 2.23 (94%) and 2.5 of 2.66 (94%). 94% as the best guess, 95% the high end. The low end, 60%, is ours, for a nuclear winter weaker than Xia et al. model (Reisner et al. 2018 find far less soot reaching the stratosphere): a war's direct deaths (about 360 million in Xia et al.'s largest US-Russia war, as reported) are then a larger share of a war that just passes the 10% threshold (814 million deaths: 56% famine). Read where work can avert only the famine (food resilience), not the blasts, fire and fallout. The famine figures already assume livestock slaughtered, feed diverted to people and trade halted.

rows.label: Pandemics: share of people who die in a catastrophe the world survives

source.title: charityevals' judgment, anchored on the tournament's 10% threshold and the deadliest pandemics on record
source.page: p. 16, Table 2 (catastrophe: over 10% of humans die within 5 years)

rows.explainer: A pandemic that kills over 10% of people: most such outcomes sit near the threshold (the 1918 influenza killed perhaps 2-5% of the world; the Black Death a third of Europe), so 15%, from the 10% threshold to 40% for an engineered pathogen. Our judgment.

rows.label: AI: share of people who die in a catastrophe the world survives

source.title: charityevals' judgment, anchored on the tournament's 10% threshold

rows.explainer: An AI catastrophe that kills over 10% of people but not everyone has no published size: a quarter, from the threshold to about two thirds. Our judgment.

rows.label: Losses beyond deaths in a catastrophe, as a share of the deaths' value

source.title: charityevals' judgment (docs/normalization.md 2.19)
source.note: Stated as a fact set to 0 so it shows.

rows.explainer: Survivors' lost income and health, injuries and the births lost while the world recovers are not counted: our judgment, stated as a fact set to 0 so it shows, the reason the default is likely low. The high end, 30% of the deaths' value, if survivors lose years of consumption. Read on every death averted, extinction-level ones included (where no one survives to lose income), so its high end overstates by a few percent; 0 at the default.

rows.label: World population now

source.title: World Bank, World Development Indicators: Population, total (SP.POP.TOTL), World, 2024

rows.explainer: The people an extinction-level catastrophe would kill, and the base of a smaller catastrophe's deaths (× catastrophe_death_share). World Bank figure from the UN's World Population Prospects.

rows.label: Life expectancy at birth, world

source.title: World Bank, World Development Indicators: Life expectancy at birth, total (SP.DYN.LE00.IN), World, 2024

rows.explainer: How long the people alive now would have lived on: over this many years the future generations' stream rises from nothing to the long-run population, so an extinction's future loss counts only people not yet born (those alive now are counted as deaths).

rows.label: AI misalignment work: share of the yearly AI extinction risk a typical $1 million removes, while it counts

source.title: Rethink Priorities, Cross-Cause Cost-Effectiveness Model, x-risk interventions (small-scale project presets)
source.page: Small-scale AI Misalignment Project: $200k-1M, 96.4% chance of no effect, else a relative cut of 1e-6 to 5.5e-5 in extinction and catastrophe risk; applied by Rethink to misalignment risk only, 90% of AI risk (ccm/world/longterm_params.py lines 87-99: 'AI default risks split as 90% misalignment and 10% misuse')

rows.explainer: Rethink Priorities' preset for a typical project against AI misalignment, as its expected value per $1 million of all AI risk: (1 − chance of no effect) × the mean relative cut ÷ the mean cost (lognormal means of its 90% ranges: the ratio of means, as a donor's average dollar, not Rethink's mean of per-project ratios) × 0.9, misalignment's share of AI risk in Rethink's model (it applies the preset's cut to misalignment risk only; the misuse tenth is untouched) × 0.772, Rethink's backfire step (a 70% chance the effect has the intended sign, harm at 30% of its size when it doesn't: (0.7 − 0.3 × 0.3) ÷ (0.7 + 0.3 × 0.3)). So a typical project's chance of doing harm is in this figure; a model's harm rows add only harms beyond a typical project's. Rethink applies the cut to each year of risk while the effect persists (15-25 years); here the years are the site's one answer, $win_years_counted, discounted. The range is ours, ten times either way: Rethink calls its x-risk inputs placeholders, and its AI figure is two orders of magnitude below its pandemic and nuclear ones (Rethink extrapolated the small project's cut linearly from its AI misalignment megaproject, OpenAI's Superalignment team at $8-28B for a 50-80% cut, and took a similar chance of no effect, 96.4% against the megaproject's 97.3%; the extinction and catastrophe cuts are drawn independently here, a slight widening). Catastrophes the world survives take Rethink's own split for them (ai_catastrophe_cut_per_million, 32% of their deaths).

rows.label: AI misalignment work: share of the yearly AI catastrophe risk a typical $1 million removes, while it counts

source.title: Rethink Priorities, Cross-Cause Cost-Effectiveness Model, x-risk interventions (small-scale project presets)
source.page: Small-scale AI Misalignment Project: $200k-1M, 96.4% chance of no effect, else a relative cut of 1e-6 to 5.5e-5 in extinction and catastrophe risk; applied by Rethink to misalignment risk only (ccm/world/longterm_params.py lines 87-99: 'AI default risks split as 90% misalignment and 10% misuse', catastrophes per extinction 2 for misalignment and 50 for misuse), share of people killed 36-96% (mean 0.66) for misalignment and 5-96% (mean 0.505) for misuse; so misalignment is 0.9 x 2 x 0.66 / (0.9 x 2 x 0.66 + 0.1 x 50 x 0.505) = 32% of the deaths in AI catastrophes the world survives

rows.explainer: Rethink Priorities' preset for a typical project against AI misalignment, as its expected value per $1 million of all AI risk: (1 − chance of no effect) × the mean relative cut ÷ the mean cost (lognormal means of its 90% ranges: the ratio of means, as a donor's average dollar, not Rethink's mean of per-project ratios) × 0.32, misalignment's share of the deaths in AI catastrophes the world survives in Rethink's model (it applies the preset's cut to misalignment risk only: misalignment is 90% of AI extinction risk, Rethink expects 2 survivable catastrophes per extinction from misalignment against 50 from misuse, and a misalignment catastrophe kills more, a mean 66% of people against 50.5%, so 0.9 × 2 × 0.66 ÷ (0.9 × 2 × 0.66 + 0.1 × 50 × 0.505)) × 0.772, Rethink's backfire step (a 70% chance the effect has the intended sign, harm at 30% of its size when it doesn't: (0.7 − 0.3 × 0.3) ÷ (0.7 + 0.3 × 0.3)). So a typical project's chance of doing harm is in this figure; a model's harm rows add only harms beyond a typical project's. Rethink applies the cut to each year of risk while the effect persists (15-25 years); here the years are the site's one answer, $win_years_counted, discounted. The range is ours, ten times either way: Rethink calls its x-risk inputs placeholders, and its AI figure is two orders of magnitude below its pandemic and nuclear ones (Rethink extrapolated the small project's cut linearly from its AI misalignment megaproject, OpenAI's Superalignment team at $8-28B for a 50-80% cut, and took a similar chance of no effect, 96.4% against the megaproject's 97.3%; the extinction and catastrophe cuts are drawn independently here, a slight widening). The tournament doesn't split catastrophes by type, so Rethink's split is used for them as it is for extinction (ai_extinction_cut_per_million takes its 90%); Rethink's misalignment ratio against the tournament's three survivable catastrophes per extinction would give about 0.6 instead, inside the range.

rows.label: AI misuse work: share of the yearly AI extinction risk a typical $1 million removes, while it counts

source.title: Rethink Priorities, Cross-Cause Cost-Effectiveness Model, x-risk interventions (small-scale project presets)
source.page: Small-scale AI Misuse Project: prob_no_effect 0.95, effect_on_xrisk lognorm 1e-4 to 5e-3, effect_on_catastrophic_risk lognorm 1e-2 to 5e-2, cost lognorm $200k-20M; applied by Rethink to misuse risk only (ccm/world/longterm_params.py: 'AI default risks split as 90% misalignment and 10% misuse', catastrophes per extinction 2 for misalignment and 50 for misuse, share of people killed mean 0.66 for misalignment and 0.505 for misuse)

rows.explainer: Rethink Priorities' preset for a typical small project against AI misuse (accidental misuse or intentional harmful use: tests of dangerous knowledge, defences against misuse), as its expected value per $1 million of all AI risk, computed exactly as ai_extinction_cut_per_million is for misalignment: (1 − chance of no effect) × the mean relative cut ÷ the mean cost (lognormal means of its 90% ranges) × 0.1, misuse's share of AI extinction risk in Rethink's model (it applies the preset's cut to misuse risk only) × 0.772, Rethink's backfire step: 0.05 × the mean extinction cut 0.00143 ÷ $5.33M × 0.1 × 0.772. A model weights it against the misalignment preset by its share of AI spending on misuse work. The range is ours, ten times either way, as for the other presets (Rethink calls its x-risk inputs placeholders).

rows.label: Cost of a year of full-time work on catastrophic risks

source.title: charityevals' judgment, anchored on AI safety field size and funding (McAleese 2025) and research organisations' Form 990s
source.note: About 1,100 full-time AI safety staff in 2025 against $110-190M of philanthropy in 2024 (McAleese) gives $100-170k a head before labs' higher pay; policy organisations' total expenses per employee run $250-300k.

rows.explainer: What an employer spends for a year of a researcher's or policy professional's work on these risks, overheads included: turns a field-building charity's added work-years into dollars of typical work, valued at the area's cut per $1 million. Our judgment.

rows.label: Years a person trained or placed in work on catastrophic risks stays in it
rows.explainer: How long the added work of someone a fellowship, course or placement brings into work on catastrophic risks lasts, before turnover or others entering in their place: about five years, 2 to 10, our judgment from the field's turnover (most of its organisations are under ten years old and staff move between them, to labs and to government). No field-wide follow-up of alumni is published. Read by every catastrophic-risk model's field-building branch (fb_work_years), discounted there at the shared rate; one figure, so the branches differ only in who is trained.

source.title: charityevals' judgment, anchored on the AI safety field's growth and age (McAleese 2025)
source.note: The field's full-time staff grew from a few hundred to about 1,100 in under a decade, so few careers in it are yet longer than ten years and many people move on to labs or government; no field-wide follow-up of fellowship alumni is published.

rows.label: Share of the land-use risk of new diseases that scales with tropical forest loss
rows.explainer: IPBES's land-use change includes farming expansion, settlement and wildlife trade as well as clearing tropical forest. Anchor: Allen et al. (2017, Nature Communications, doi 10.1038/s41467-017-00923-8) find emerging-disease hotspots best predicted by tropical forest regions with high mammal diversity undergoing land-use change, so clearing tropical forest is a large part, not all, of the land-use risk. Our judgment: half of it scales with tropical forest loss, in proportion to the hectares lost (10-100%); Dobson et al. (Science, 2020) argue for cutting deforestation as pandemic prevention but give no dose-response. Read by every forest model's pandemic-risk rows; the least grounded number in them.

rows.label: Share of every later year's healthy life a COVID-scale pandemic would take
rows.explainer: 0: the world recovers from a COVID-scale pandemic; its deaths are counted as deaths. The tiny high end (one in a hundred thousand) allows for lasting damage. Our judgment, read by every model that counts a COVID-scale pandemic averted.
